]}","refusal":null,"reasoning":"Let me rate each dossier on the scale, higher is safer.

Dossier 1: No criminalisation, no LGR (resident gap), no protections naming gender identity, thin data, stigmatisation general, no documented trans incidents, no documented traveler-facing restrictions. Decriminalized same-sex conduct. Open questions on document mismatch (no remedy but no documented friction either — officials don't doubt foreign documents; there's no documented rejection). Rule 1 says absence of LGR machinery doesn't reach visitors unless documented. So this is mostly thin data with mild societal stigma. Score ~0.60-0.65. Thin-data extrapolation: criminalisation absent, no documented targeting, no acceptance documented. Stigmatisation general. I'd say 0.62.

Dossier 2: Wartime country — male-marker holders stopped at the border (documented traveler-facing exposure at border!). Wait: "holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the national border guard service" — but that's about mobilization/emigration restrictions under martial law, applying to male markers generally (all men), not trans-specific. But for a trans visitor with male marker... Actually a trans visitor wouldn't be subject to mobilization, but border stops of male markers — that's a documented border friction. It affects anyone with a male marker leaving/entering? Actually it's about citizens being stopped from leaving. For a trans visitor it's borderline. Document friction for trans people: NGO helps with document reissue for legal border crossing — suggests document friction.

Positives: legal gender recognition exists, employment anti-discrimination on gender identity, media hate-speech ban, rising acceptance (70% rights support), pride held with heavy police protection, court recognition of same-sex couples, functioning civil society.

Negatives: documented police tolerance of violence (dated 2011-2013), most recent violent incident 2012, trans diagnosis gatekeeping (resident), draft civil code hostile (not law), religious/social hostility (Orthodox church, ex-gay movement), constitutional marriage definition.

The violence record is dated (2011-2013). Recent signals: acceptance polling rising, court rulings protecting, pride with police protection. Rule of law functioning (courts ruling for couples). Military commission humiliating assessment for diagnosis — resident-facing mostly but also affects border crossing for male markers.

Wartime context: general war is out of scope. But border stops of male-marker holders — for a trans visitor, if their marker is male, they might be stopped? The dossier says "holders of male gender markers have been stopped at the border by the national border guard service" — this applies to citizens under martial law emigration restrictions. A foreign visitor isn't subject to mobilization. Still it's a document-friction signal.

Score maybe 0.62-0.68. Given functioning institutions, documented protections in force (employment discrimination ban, media bill), rising acceptance, pride operating with police protection, but documented social hostility and dated violence with police impunity. I'd say ~0.65.

Dossier 3: No criminalisation, no LGR (highest court bans it — resident gap but with regional court pressure), education law banning "propaganda" of non-traditional orientation and gender identity (Aug 2024, in force) — this is a state hostility signal but aimed at education, not directly travelers. Survey: 46% avoid locations for fear of assault, only 27% open about being LGBTIQ — strong hostile day-to-day climate. Hate crimes poorly investigated (2015, pattern carried forward). Violence: 2008 killing, 2020 assault of minors, pride attacked 2008. Municipal ban on public demonstration of orientation (upheld on appeal 2011, status unknown).

Survey-measured discrimination/avoidance prevalence: 46% avoid locations for fear of assault — that's LGBTIQ-wide, about fear of assault — this is a current (2024) everyday-exposure signal. Rule 21: survey-measured discrimination prevalence where a majority or large plurality report identity-related discrimination is primary everyday-exposure tier. 46% avoid locations, 28% felt discriminated — large plurality. Also 27% open only.

Also state threat-framing: education law prohibiting promotion of gender identity — tier: state hostility. Also no facility laws documented. Same-sex decriminalized 1968.

Score: hostile climate, hate-crime enforcement failure, no LGR by constitutional ruling (resident), no documented traveler-facing restrictions at border. Compared to dossier 2: dossier 3 has stronger societal hostility (survey), state propaganda law, poor hate-crime investigation. Dossier 2 has documented protections and rising acceptance, but documented police impunity (dated) and border stops.

I'd put dossier 3 below dossier 2: ~0.55-0.58.

Dossier 4: Documented state-tolerated/state-directed targeting: police raids detaining 100+ with beatings, forced medical exams, blackmail, 60 imprisoned/fined (2017); 2023 private party raid with forced medical examinations, sexual harassment, threats of outing; trans woman murdered March 2024 with inadequate police investigation; ranked last 49/49; no discrimination protections; no gender marker change; 77% hateful media; state-affiliated TV hate speech. This is tier 2 (state-tolerated targeting, police raids) — organized targeting by police. Score low: ~0.25-0.30. Police raids on queer venues with forced exams and imprisonment — that's tier 1/2. A trans visitor outed faces police detention risk. Score ~0.25.

Dossier 5: No criminalisation, no trans framework, no LGR (resident gap), no protections, but "no reported violent incidents" (2012, dated), society "relatively tolerant of consensual same-sex conduct" with social taboos, some cases of violence (2018), 2010 survey among more tolerant. General security context: coup, arbitrary killings, torture, impunity tied to drug-trafficking corruption — rule of law poor. Rule 8: general crime out of scope unless it raises trans-specific risk (collapse of police protection). Torture by security forces and impunity — that's general state violence; does it reach trans people? Not documented specifically. Thin data. Structural signals: no criminalisation, no recognition machinery, no documented targeting of trans, social tolerance mild, but weak rule of law and thin data with a coup context.

Extrapolation: no criminalisation is a real positive; no documented hostility toward trans specifically; general stigma but tolerance. Poor rule of law means paper protections weak — but there aren't many protections anyway. The absence of documented incidents is thin data. I'd say ~0.55-0.60. Given documented social tolerance ("relatively tolerant"), decriminalization, no state targeting documented, but no protections, no recognition, dated data, weak rule of law, and some violence cases 2018: ~0.57.

Hmm, compare dossier 1 and 5: Dossier 1 — decriminalized 2012, employment protection (orientation), hate-crime sentencing (orientation), stigmatisation, poll 46% wouldn't mind LGBTQ neighbor (i.e., slim majority would mind — actually 46% would like or not mind; so 54% would mind — mild negativity). Thin data, no documented trans incidents. No documented acceptance.

Dossier 5 — tolerance documented (2012 report "relatively tolerant"), 2010 survey among more tolerant, but 2018 NGO reports violence cases, no protections at all, weak rule of law (coup, torture, impunity).

Both are thin. Dossier 1 has some protections (orientation-based) — climate signals. Dossier 5 has documented relative tolerance. I'd put them close: Dossier 1 ~0.62, Dossier 5 ~0.58 (weaker rule of law raises severity if something happens — impunity context).

Actually, does dossier 5's general impunity/torture context raise trans-specific risk? Rule 8 says general violence out of scope unless independently raising trans-specific risk (collapse of police protection for a targeted group). Dossier 5 doesn't document targeting of trans people, so mostly out of scope. But it colors severity — if a trans visitor is assaulted, recourse likely absent. That's a mild deduction.

Let me settle scores:
1: 0.62
2: 0.66
3: 0.55
4: 0.25
5: 0.57

Check ordering logic: Dossier 2 vs 3. Dossier 2: documented protections in force (employment GI discrimination ban, media hate speech ban), LGR without surgery, rising acceptance 70%, pride operating, courts recognizing couples. But: border stops of male markers (martial law — citizenship-focused), humiliating military commission, draft civil code hostile, social/religious hostility, dated police impunity. Dossier 3: constitutional ban on LGR, education propaganda law in force (state hostility toward gender identity), survey showing 46% avoid locations, 27% open, hate-crime investigation failures, pride needs heavy police guard, far-right violence. Dossier 3's state is actively hostile (education law naming gender identity), plus strong societal hostility survey. Dossier 2's state is protective-ish with documented protections. So 2 > 3 clearly. Maybe 2: 0.67, 3: 0.54.

Forced medical exams and blackmail by police = tier 2. 0.25 seems right (High Risk band).

Dossier 1 vs 5: 1 has employment/hate-crime protections (orientation) as climate; stigmatisation; poll showing slight majority would mind LGBTQ neighbor. 5 has documented relative tolerance but total absence of protections and weak rule of law. Both thin. I'll give 1: 0.62, 5: 0.58.
